title: Sum of Values Seen Once
statement:
You get an integer array nums. A value is lonely if it occurs in the array exactly once.

Return the sum of all lonely values. A value that occurs two or more times adds nothing at all, not even one copy. If no value is lonely, return 0.

examples.why: 9 and 2 occur once each. Both 4s are left out, not just the second one.
The only value occurs three times, so nothing is lonely.
Counting distinct values would give 5 + 1 + 8 = 14. Only 8 occurs exactly once.

hints: For each value you need one fact: how many times does it occur in the whole array?
Counting by rescanning the array for every element costs O(n²). Count everything once instead.
Build a count map in one pass, then add up the keys whose count is exactly 1.

explain.intuition:
Whether a value is lonely depends on the whole array, not on what you have seen so far. A 4 that looks lonely at index 0 stops being lonely when another 4 shows up later. So first count, then decide.

A frequency map does the counting in one pass. It is the same move as grouping events by type before you render a summary: you cannot label a group until you have seen all of it.
steps: Create an empty map from value to count.
Walk nums and increment the count of each value.
Walk the map. Add each key whose count is exactly 1 to the total.
pitfalls: Adding a value when first seen and subtracting it when seen the second time. A third copy then adds it back, so [6, 6, 6] gives 6 instead of 0.
Summing distinct values (one copy of each) instead of values that occur exactly once.

solutions.title: Count each element by rescanning
solutions.idea: For every position, count how often its value occurs in the whole array. Add it when the count is 1.

solutions.title: Frequency map
solutions.idea: Count every value in one pass, then sum the values whose count is exactly 1.

followups: Can you do it in a single pass, adjusting the total as counts change?
Values are bounded by 100 000. How would a plain array of counts compare with a hash map here?
